board_events.text: READING AN RQ: (1) write or recall the balanced respiration equation for the substrate; (2) read off CO2 produced and O2 consumed from the coefficients; (3) divide CO2 by O2. The RQ is decided by ONE thing: how oxygen-rich the molecule already is.
A carbohydrate already carries oxygen in roughly the proportion needed, so it consumes exactly as much O2 as it releases CO2 - RQ = 1.

A fat is a long, oxygen-poor hydrocarbon chain; oxidising all that carbon and hydrogen demands a lot of extra O2, so O2 consumed exceeds CO2 released - RQ $\lt$ 1 (about 0.7). An organic acid is the opposite - already partly oxidised and oxygen-rich - so it needs very little external O2 - RQ $\gt$ 1.
In anaerobic respiration the cell releases CO2 but uses no oxygen at all, so the denominator is zero and RQ becomes infinite. A sealed flask of fermenting yeast is the classic demonstration.
CAUTION: living tissues rarely burn one pure fuel. A measured RQ is an AVERAGE - read it as evidence of the dominant substrate, not proof of a single one.

WHY AMPHIBOLIC, step by step: to build membranes the cell withdraws acetyl CoA to synthesise fatty acids; to build proteins it withdraws alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate to make amino acids by transamination. Every withdrawal must be balanced by replenishment, or the cycle runs dry.

Because the same intermediates are both consumed for energy and exported for construction, respiration cannot be labelled purely catabolic. It is not an isolated furnace but the CENTRAL EXCHANGE of the cell's chemistry, linking carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism - which is why it closes the chapter.

segments.text: <curious> This is the last subtopic, and it does two jobs at once. It fixes two loose ends we have quietly left dangling all chapter.
The board holds the first idea. One pathway, two directions of traffic. Keep an eye on the green arrows, because they are the whole point.
So far we have treated respiration as a one-way demolition. Take glucose, knock it apart, collect the energy. That picture is true, but it is incomplete, and the incompleteness matters.

Start with a kitchen. A household kitchen is not only a place where food is broken down for eating. The same counter, the same knives, the same stove are also used to assemble dishes from raw ingredients. The respiratory pathway is exactly this kind of dual-purpose kitchen.

It is mostly catabolic. It breaks molecules down to release energy. But the cell also reaches into the very same pathway to pull out intermediates and build new things. Acetyl coenzyme A is siphoned off to make fatty acids. Alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate are withdrawn to make amino acids. Because the pathway runs breakdown and build-up traffic on the same road, we call it amphibolic. Amphi means both. Neither purely catabolic nor purely anabolic.

Now the second loose end. Glucose is not the only fuel a plant cell can feed into respiration. When sugars run low, say in a germinating castor seed packed with stored oil, the cell burns fats, and even proteins instead.

Here is how they get in. Fats are split into glycerol and fatty acids. Glycerol slips into glycolysis. Fatty acids are chopped into acetyl coenzyme A. Proteins are broken down to amino acids, and those, after losing their nitrogen, enter as pyruvate, as acetyl coenzyme A, or as Krebs cycle intermediates.

And notice the pattern. Every fuel funnels toward one great central junction. Acetyl coenzyme A. And from there into the Krebs cycle. The respiratory pathway is a universal furnace that accepts carbohydrate, fat and protein alike. That single junction is worth a question all by itself.

Which immediately raises a practical question for a plant physiologist. If a tissue could be burning sugar, or oil, or acid, how do we tell which one? The trick is to measure the gases. Different fuels need different amounts of oxygen and release different amounts of carbon dioxide. The ratio of the two, carbon dioxide out over oxygen in, is the respiratory quotient, and it acts like a chemical fingerprint of the fuel.
Now the definitions, and this subtopic is compact but reliably tested. The whole thing rests on two ideas and one table.

The table is on the board, and it is the must-memorise block of the subtopic. But do not memorise it yet. Read the why column, because in a moment we will replace the whole table with a single principle.

First definition. An amphibolic pathway is a metabolic pathway that serves both catabolism, meaning degradation and energy release, and anabolism, meaning the synthesis of building blocks. Both, in the same pathway, at the same time.

And the reason respiration qualifies. Intermediates such as acetyl coenzyme A, alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate are simultaneously broken down for energy and drawn off to build fats and amino acids. Note the word simultaneously. It is not that the pathway switches modes. Both things happen at once.

Now the respiratory substrates, and their entry points, which is a table C U E T likes. Carbohydrate breaks down to glucose and enters at glycolysis. Fat breaks down to glycerol plus fatty acids. Glycerol goes into glycolysis, and fatty acids become acetyl coenzyme A by beta oxidation. Protein breaks down to amino acids, which enter as pyruvate, as acetyl coenzyme A, or as Krebs intermediates, after deamination. Notice that fats and proteins bypass the early part of glycolysis entirely.

Second definition. The respiratory quotient, R Q, is the ratio of the volume of carbon dioxide evolved to the volume of oxygen consumed in respiration over the same period. Over the same period matters. It is a rate ratio, measured across one window of time.

<whisper> And one clean fact that gets asked directly. R Q is a pure ratio. It is dimensionless, with no unit. Volume divided by volume cancels. That is the only dimensional remark this entire subtopic needs, so it is easy marks if the question comes.

And here are the values. Carbohydrate gives exactly one. Protein is roughly zero point eight to zero point nine. Fat is about zero point seven. Organic acids are greater than one, with malic acid at about one point three three and oxalic acid at about four. And anaerobic respiration gives infinity. Look at the spread for a second, because the pattern in that column is about to become the only thing you need to remember.
<excited> Now the promised move. We are going to throw away the R Q table and replace it with one question you can ask in a single glance.
The board shows the convergence funnel. Three fuels across the top, all arriving at acetyl coenzyme A. And watch the green arrows, which point the other way.

First, how to read an R Q. The procedure is three steps. Write or recall the balanced respiration equation for the substrate. Read off carbon dioxide produced and oxygen consumed straight from the coefficients. Divide carbon dioxide by oxygen. That is it. But the deeper point is this. The R Q of a fuel is decided by exactly one thing. How oxygen-rich the molecule already is.

Work it through. A carbohydrate like glucose already carries oxygen in roughly the proportion needed. So it consumes exactly as much oxygen as it releases carbon dioxide. R Q equals one. The sugar brings its own oxygen to the party.

A fat is a long, oxygen-poor hydrocarbon chain. Oxidising all that carbon and hydrogen demands a lot of extra oxygen from outside. So oxygen consumed exceeds carbon dioxide released, and R Q drops below one, to about zero point seven. An organic acid is the exact opposite. It is already partly oxidised, already oxygen-rich, so it needs very little external oxygen, and R Q climbs above one. Same logic, opposite direction.

And the extreme case. In anaerobic respiration the cell releases carbon dioxide, in alcoholic fermentation for example, but uses no oxygen at all. So the denominator is zero, and R Q becomes infinite. This is why a sealed flask of fermenting yeast is the classic R Q equals infinity demonstration. It is not a trick. It is division by zero.

Now an honest caution, because those neat values describe a tissue burning one pure fuel, and living tissues rarely oblige. They usually oxidise carbohydrates, fats and proteins simultaneously, so a measured R Q is an average of whatever mixture is being respired. A germinating oilseed may show an R Q that drifts upward over days as it converts stored fat into sugars and starts respiring those. So read an R Q as evidence of the dominant substrate, not proof of a single one. N E E T occasionally probes this by giving an in-between value and asking what it implies.

Back to the amphibolic idea, step by step. Normally the cycle runs catabolically. But when a cell needs to build membranes, it withdraws acetyl coenzyme A to synthesise fatty acids. When it needs to build proteins, it withdraws alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate to make amino acids by transamination. And every withdrawal for synthesis must be balanced by replenishment, otherwise the cycle would run dry. Remember, O A A has to be there to catch the next acetyl coenzyme A.

So because the same intermediates are both consumed for energy and exported for construction, the respiratory pathway cannot be labelled purely catabolic. It is amphibolic. And this dual character is what gives a cell its metabolic flexibility. It can switch fuels when sugar is scarce, and it can divert carbon skeletons out of respiration whenever growth or repair demands new fatty acids or amino acids. In that sense respiration is not an isolated furnace. It is the central exchange of the cell's chemistry, linking carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism through a shared set of intermediates. That integration is the deeper reason this appears as the final, unifying topic of the chapter.
<curious> यह आख़िरी subtopic है, और यह एक साथ दो काम करता है। यह उन दो loose ends को बाँधता है जिन्हें हमने पूरे chapter चुपचाप लटका रखा था।
Board पर पहला idea है। एक pathway, traffic की दो दिशाएँ। हरे arrows पर नज़र रखिए, क्योंकि पूरी बात वही है।
अब तक हमने respiration को एक-तरफ़ा तोड़फोड़ माना है। Glucose लीजिए, तोड़िए, energy बटोरिए। यह तस्वीर सही है, लेकिन अधूरी है, और यह अधूरापन मायने रखता है।

एक kitchen से शुरू कीजिए। घर की kitchen सिर्फ़ वह जगह नहीं जहाँ खाना खाने के लिए तोड़ा जाता है। वही counter, वही चाकू, वही चूल्हा कच्ची सामग्री से dishes जोड़ने में भी काम आते हैं। Respiratory pathway ठीक इसी तरह की dual-purpose kitchen है।

यह ज़्यादातर catabolic है। यह molecules तोड़कर energy छोड़ती है। लेकिन cell उसी pathway में हाथ डालकर intermediates खींच लेती है और नई चीज़ें बनाती है। Acetyl coenzyme A निकालकर fatty acids बनाए जाते हैं। Alpha-ketoglutarate और oxaloacetate खींचकर amino acids बनते हैं। चूँकि pathway एक ही सड़क पर तोड़ने और जोड़ने, दोनों की traffic चलाती है, इसे amphibolic कहते हैं। Amphi यानी दोनों। न पूरी तरह catabolic, न पूरी तरह anabolic।

अब दूसरा loose end। Glucose ही इकलौता fuel नहीं जो plant cell respiration में डाल सकती है। जब sugars कम पड़ जाएँ, जैसे तेल से भरे castor seed के अंकुरण में, तो cell fats, और यहाँ तक कि proteins भी जलाती है।

ये अंदर कैसे घुसते हैं, यह देखिए। Fats टूटकर glycerol और fatty acids बनते हैं। Glycerol glycolysis में फिसल जाता है। Fatty acids कटकर acetyl coenzyme A बन जाते हैं। Proteins टूटकर amino acids बनते हैं, और वे अपनी nitrogen खोने के बाद pyruvate, acetyl coenzyme A, या Krebs cycle के intermediates के रूप में घुसते हैं।

और pattern देखिए। हर fuel एक ही बड़े केंद्रीय junction की ओर बहता है। Acetyl coenzyme A। और वहाँ से Krebs cycle में। Respiratory pathway एक universal भट्ठी है जो carbohydrate, fat और protein, सबको स्वीकार करती है। वह अकेला junction ही अपने आप में एक सवाल के लायक़ है।

और इससे plant physiologist के सामने तुरंत एक व्यावहारिक सवाल खड़ा होता है। अगर कोई tissue चीनी जला सकता है, तेल भी, या acid भी, तो पता कैसे चले कि जल क्या रहा है? तरकीब है gases मापिए। अलग fuels को अलग मात्रा में oxygen चाहिए और वे अलग मात्रा में carbon dioxide छोड़ते हैं। इन दोनों का अनुपात, यानी carbon dioxide बाहर बटा oxygen अंदर, respiratory quotient है, और यह fuel की chemical उँगली की छाप की तरह काम करता है।
अब definitions, और यह subtopic छोटा है लेकिन भरोसे से पूछा जाता है। पूरी बात दो ideas और एक table पर टिकी है।
Table board पर है, और यही इस subtopic का must-memorise block है। लेकिन अभी रटिए मत। why वाला column पढ़िए, क्योंकि थोड़ी देर में हम पूरी table की जगह एक ही सिद्धांत रख देंगे।
पहली definition। Amphibolic pathway वह metabolic pathway है जो catabolism, यानी तोड़ना और energy छोड़ना, तथा anabolism, यानी building blocks बनाना, दोनों करती है। दोनों, एक ही pathway में, एक ही समय।

और respiration इसमें आती क्यों है। Acetyl coenzyme A, alpha-ketoglutarate और oxaloacetate जैसे intermediates एक साथ energy के लिए तोड़े भी जाते हैं और fats तथा amino acids बनाने के लिए खींचे भी जाते हैं। एक साथ शब्द पर ध्यान दीजिए। ऐसा नहीं कि pathway mode बदलती है। दोनों काम एक ही वक़्त होते हैं।

अब respiratory substrates और उनके entry points, यह table C U E T को पसंद है। Carbohydrate टूटकर glucose बनता है और glycolysis पर घुसता है। Fat टूटकर glycerol और fatty acids बनता है। Glycerol glycolysis में जाता है, और fatty acids beta oxidation से acetyl coenzyme A बन जाते हैं। Protein टूटकर amino acids बनता है, जो deamination के बाद pyruvate, acetyl coenzyme A, या Krebs intermediates के रूप में घुसते हैं। ध्यान दीजिए कि fats और proteins glycolysis का शुरुआती हिस्सा पूरी तरह छोड़ देते हैं।

दूसरी definition। Respiratory quotient, यानी R Q, respiration में उसी अवधि के दौरान निकली carbon dioxide के आयतन और खपत हुई oxygen के आयतन का अनुपात है। उसी अवधि वाली बात मायने रखती है। यह एक rate ratio है, समय की एक ही खिड़की में मापा गया।

<whisper> और एक साफ़ fact जो सीधे पूछा जाता है। R Q एक शुद्ध अनुपात है। यह dimensionless है, इसका कोई unit नहीं। आयतन बटा आयतन कट जाता है। इस पूरे subtopic में यही एकमात्र dimensional बात है, तो सवाल आया तो आसान marks हैं।

और ये रहे values। Carbohydrate देता है ठीक एक। Protein लगभग zero point eight से zero point nine। Fat लगभग zero point seven। Organic acids एक से ज़्यादा, जिनमें malic acid लगभग one point three three और oxalic acid लगभग चार। और anaerobic respiration देती है infinity। एक पल इस फैलाव को देखिए, क्योंकि उस column का pattern ही अब वह इकलौती चीज़ बनने वाला है जो आपको याद रखनी है।
<excited> अब वह वादा किया हुआ क़दम। हम R Q की table फेंकने वाले हैं और उसकी जगह एक ऐसा सवाल रखने वाले हैं जो एक नज़र में पूछा जा सके।
Board पर convergence funnel है। ऊपर तीन fuels, और सब acetyl coenzyme A पर पहुँचते हुए। और हरे arrows देखिए, जो दूसरी दिशा में जाते हैं।

पहले, R Q पढ़ना कैसे है। तरीक़ा तीन steps का है। Substrate के लिए balanced respiration equation लिखिए या याद कीजिए। Coefficients से सीधे पढ़िए कि कितनी carbon dioxide बनी और कितनी oxygen ख़र्च हुई। Carbon dioxide को oxygen से भाग दीजिए। बस। लेकिन गहरी बात यह है। किसी fuel का R Q ठीक एक चीज़ से तय होता है। वह molecule ख़ुद कितना oxygen से भरा है।

इसे चलाकर देखिए। Glucose जैसा carbohydrate पहले से लगभग उतना ही oxygen लिए चलता है जितना चाहिए। तो वह ठीक उतनी ही oxygen खर्च करता है जितनी carbon dioxide छोड़ता है। R Q बराबर एक। चीनी अपनी oxygen ख़ुद लेकर आती है।

Fat एक लंबी, oxygen-ग़रीब hydrocarbon chain है। उस सारे carbon और hydrogen को जलाने के लिए बाहर से बहुत ज़्यादा oxygen चाहिए। तो खपत हुई oxygen निकली carbon dioxide से ज़्यादा हो जाती है, और R Q एक से नीचे, लगभग zero point seven पर आ जाता है। Organic acid बिल्कुल उल्टा है। वह पहले से आंशिक रूप से oxidised है, oxygen से भरपूर, तो उसे बाहरी oxygen बहुत कम चाहिए, और R Q एक से ऊपर चढ़ जाता है। वही logic, उल्टी दिशा।

और चरम मामला। Anaerobic respiration में cell carbon dioxide छोड़ती है, जैसे alcoholic fermentation में, लेकिन oxygen बिल्कुल इस्तेमाल नहीं करती। तो हर बराबर शून्य, और R Q अनंत हो जाता है। इसीलिए हवा से बंद fermenting yeast का flask R Q बराबर infinity का classic प्रदर्शन है। यह कोई चाल नहीं। यह शून्य से भाग है।

अब एक ईमानदार चेतावनी, क्योंकि वे साफ़-सुथरे values उस tissue के हैं जो एक शुद्ध fuel जला रहा हो, और जीवित tissues शायद ही ऐसा करते हैं। वे आम तौर पर carbohydrates, fats और proteins एक साथ oxidise करते हैं, तो मापा गया R Q उस मिश्रण का औसत होता है जो उस वक़्त जल रहा है। अंकुरित होते oilseed का R Q दिनों के साथ ऊपर खिसक सकता है, क्योंकि वह जमा fat को शक्कर में बदलकर उन्हें जलाने लगता है। तो R Q को प्रमुख substrate का सबूत मानिए, किसी एक ही substrate का प्रमाण नहीं। N E E T कभी-कभी बीच का value देकर पूछ लेता है कि इसका क्या मतलब है।

अब वापस amphibolic idea पर, क़दम दर क़दम। आम तौर पर cycle catabolically चलती है। लेकिन जब cell को membranes बनानी हों, तो वह acetyl coenzyme A खींचकर fatty acids बनाती है। जब proteins बनाने हों, तो वह alpha-ketoglutarate और oxaloacetate खींचकर transamination से amino acids बनाती है। और synthesis के लिए हुई हर निकासी की भरपाई होनी चाहिए, वरना cycle सूख जाएगी। याद रखिए, अगले acetyl coenzyme A को पकड़ने के लिए O A A वहाँ होना ही चाहिए।

तो चूँकि वही intermediates energy के लिए खर्च भी होते हैं और निर्माण के लिए बाहर भी भेजे जाते हैं, respiratory pathway को पूरी तरह catabolic नहीं कहा जा सकता। वह amphibolic है। और यही दोहरा चरित्र cell को उसका metabolic लचीलापन देता है। शक्कर कम हो तो वह fuel बदल सकती है, और growth या repair के लिए नए fatty acids या amino acids चाहिए हों तो वह carbon skeletons respiration से बाहर मोड़ सकती है। इस अर्थ में respiration कोई अलग-थलग भट्ठी नहीं। वह cell की रसायन-विद्या का केंद्रीय exchange है, जो carbohydrate, fat और protein metabolism को साझा intermediates से जोड़ता है। यही गहरी वजह है कि यह chapter का आख़िरी, जोड़ने वाला topic है।

board_events.text: Under the idealised assumptions, tally the carriers per glucose, then convert using NADH = 3 ATP and FADH2 = 2 ATP.
GLYCOLYSIS: 2 ATP direct, 2 NADH. LINK REACTION (x2): 2 NADH. KREBS CYCLE (x2 turns): 2 ATP direct, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2. TOTALS: 4 direct ATP, 10 NADH, 2 FADH2.
ETS CONVERSION: 10 x 3 = 30 ATP (from NADH), plus 2 x 2 = 4 ATP (from FADH2) = 34 ATP. Add the 4 direct: NET $\approx$ 38 ATP per glucose.

If cytoplasmic glycolytic NADH is ferried in by a shuttle that yields only 2 ATP each, the total drops to about 36 - which is why some books quote 36. Energy actually trapped: roughly 40% efficiency; the rest is lost as heat.

This figure rests on four explicit idealisations, and naming them is itself an exam point: (i) the pathway runs as a single, orderly sequence - glycolysis, then link and Krebs, then ETS - each step neatly feeding the next.

(ii) the NADH generated in the cytoplasm during glycolysis is ferried intact into the mitochondrion and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation; (iii) no intermediate is withdrawn at any stage to build some other molecule; (iv) glucose is the only substrate, with nothing else entering at intermediary points.
Real cells violate (iii) and (iv) constantly - which is precisely the amphibolic behaviour just described - so the true yield is always somewhat lower. Treat 38 as a CEILING, not a guarantee.

board_events.text: Starch yields glucose, a carbohydrate. Balanced: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 gives 6 CO2 + 6 H2O. CO2 evolved = 6; O2 consumed = 6. RQ = 6/6 = 1.
RQ = 1 is the signature of a carbohydrate substrate.
Example 2 [CUET / NEET Speed Trap]: a castor seed germinating in a sealed respirometer
Predict its RQ relative to 1, with reasoning, WITHOUT any calculation.
Oil = fat = oxygen-poor, highly reduced molecule. Oxidising it fully demands extra O2 drawn in from outside, so O2 consumed $\gt$ CO2 released. Therefore RQ $\lt$ 1 - about 0.7 for typical fats.
TRAP: assuming 'a seed, therefore RQ = 1'. That holds only for STARCHY seeds (wheat, rice). Oily seeds (castor, mustard, groundnut) give RQ $\lt$ 1. The SUBSTRATE, not the organ, decides RQ.

segments.text: Now the capstone of the whole chapter. The respiratory balance sheet. Everything we have counted for four subtopics finally gets added up.
The board has the full sheet. Follow it stage by stage as we go, because the arithmetic is simple but the bookkeeping is where marks get lost.

Under the idealised assumptions, the method is two moves. Tally the carriers per glucose, then convert them at the E T S using the rates we established. N A D H gives three A T P, F A D H two gives two A T P.

So the tally. Glycolysis gives two A T P direct and two N A D H. The link reaction, which runs twice because there are two pyruvate, gives two N A D H and no direct A T P. The Krebs cycle, two turns, gives two A T P direct, six N A D H and two F A D H two. Add the columns. Four direct A T P, ten N A D H, and two F A D H two. Those three numbers are the whole balance sheet.

Now convert. Ten N A D H times three is thirty A T P. Two F A D H two times two is four A T P. That is thirty-four from the E T S. Add the four direct ones you already had, and the net is approximately thirty-eight A T P per glucose. And notice the proportion. Thirty-four out of thirty-eight comes from the E T S. The direct A T P are almost a rounding error.

<whisper> Two footnotes worth carrying. If the cytoplasmic glycolytic N A D H is ferried in by a shuttle that yields only two A T P each instead of three, the total drops to about thirty-six. That is why some books quote thirty-six and others thirty-eight. Neither is wrong. And the energy actually trapped works out to roughly forty percent efficiency. The rest is lost as heat.

Now the part that separates a full-mark answer from a half-mark one. This figure rests on four explicit idealisations, and naming them is itself an exam point. First, the pathway is assumed to run as a single, orderly sequence. Glycolysis, then the link reaction and Krebs cycle, then the E T S, with each step neatly feeding the next.

Second, the N A D H generated in the cytoplasm during glycolysis is assumed to be ferried intact into the mitochondrion and to undergo oxidative phosphorylation. Third, no intermediate is assumed to be withdrawn at any stage to build some other molecule. And fourth, glucose is assumed to be the only substrate, with nothing else entering at intermediary points.

And now look at what this subtopic has just taught you. Real cells violate the third and fourth assumptions constantly. That is precisely the amphibolic behaviour we described a moment ago. Intermediates are withdrawn all the time, and other fuels enter all the time. So the true yield is always somewhat lower than thirty-eight. Treat thirty-eight as a ceiling, not a guarantee. That one sentence is the difference between reciting a number and understanding it.
This subtopic has exactly one formula, and then a set of substituted cases. Let us write them properly.
Here is the definition.
And carry the dimensional note with it. It is a pure ratio, dimensionless, no unit. Volume over volume.
Now the clean case. Glucose, a carbohydrate.
Read the coefficients. Six carbon dioxide evolved, six oxygen consumed. Six over six is one. This is why carbohydrate is the reference point of the whole table.
Now a fat. Tripalmitin, which is the standard textbook example.
Look at those numbers for a moment. One hundred forty-five oxygen consumed, but only one hundred two carbon dioxide released. The oxygen demand is enormous compared to the carbon dioxide output.

So the ratio comes out as one hundred two over one hundred forty-five, which is zero point seven zero three, or about zero point seven. That is not a coincidence, and it is not something to memorise separately. It falls out of the equation.

And for reference, the full set. Carbohydrate equals one. Protein zero point eight to zero point nine. Fat zero point seven. Organic acids above one, with malic at one point three three and oxalic at four. Anaerobic, infinity. But hold on to these lightly, because we are about to derive all of them from a single idea.

Example one is a straightforward board question, and it is the reference case for everything else. A germinating wheat grain respires using stored starch. Write the overall equation for glucose oxidation and calculate its respiratory quotient.
The board shows the principle we will lean on for both examples. Oxygen-poor on the left, oxygen-rich on the right.

Start by identifying the substrate, because that is always step one. Starch yields glucose, which is a carbohydrate. The balanced equation is glucose plus six oxygen gives six carbon dioxide plus six water. Now read the coefficients. Carbon dioxide evolved is six. Oxygen consumed is six. So R Q is six over six, which is one.
And state the conclusion in words, because that is what earns the mark. R Q equal to one is the signature of a carbohydrate substrate.
Example two is a C U E T and N E E T speed trap, and it is designed to be answered in about ten seconds. A castor seed, rich in stored oil, is germinating in a sealed respirometer.
Predict its R Q relative to one, with reasoning, and without any calculation. Notice the instruction. You are not meant to compute anything. You are meant to reason from the fuel.

So reason it. Oil is fat. Fat is an oxygen-poor, highly reduced molecule. Oxidising it fully demands extra oxygen drawn in from outside. So oxygen consumed is greater than carbon dioxide released. Therefore R Q is less than one, about zero point seven for typical fats. Three sentences, no arithmetic.

<curious> And here is the trap the question is actually built around. Students assume, a seed, therefore R Q equals one. But that holds only for starchy seeds, like wheat and rice. Oily seeds, castor, mustard, groundnut, give R Q less than one. The substrate decides R Q, not the organ. Whenever a question names a structure rather than a molecule, ask what is actually being burned inside it.
अब पूरे chapter का capstone। Respiratory balance sheet। चार subtopics से हम जो कुछ गिनते आए हैं, वह आख़िरकार जुड़ता है।
Board पर पूरी sheet है। साथ-साथ stage दर stage follow कीजिए, क्योंकि गणित आसान है लेकिन marks हिसाब-किताब में ही गिरते हैं।

Idealised मान्यताओं के तहत तरीक़ा दो चालों का है। प्रति glucose carriers की गिनती कीजिए, फिर उन्हें E T S पर उन दरों से बदलिए जो हम तय कर चुके हैं। N A D H देती है तीन A T P, F A D H two देती है दो A T P।

तो गिनती। Glycolysis देती है दो A T P सीधे और दो N A D H। Link reaction, जो दो बार चलती है क्योंकि pyruvate दो हैं, देती है दो N A D H और कोई सीधी A T P नहीं। Krebs cycle, दो turns, देती है दो A T P सीधे, छह N A D H और दो F A D H two। Columns जोड़िए। चार सीधी A T P, दस N A D H, और दो F A D H two। यही तीन numbers पूरी balance sheet हैं।

अब बदलिए। दस N A D H गुणा तीन बराबर तीस A T P। दो F A D H two गुणा दो बराबर चार A T P। यानी E T S से चौंतीस। इसमें वे चार सीधी A T P जोड़िए जो पहले से थीं, और net निकलता है लगभग अड़तीस A T P प्रति glucose। और अनुपात देखिए। अड़तीस में से चौंतीस E T S से आती हैं। सीधी A T P तो लगभग गिनती में ही नहीं।

<whisper> दो footnotes साथ रखिए। अगर glycolysis की cytoplasmic N A D H को कोई shuttle अंदर पहुँचाए जो तीन के बजाय सिर्फ़ दो A T P दे, तो कुल घटकर लगभग छत्तीस रह जाता है। इसीलिए कुछ किताबें छत्तीस लिखती हैं और कुछ अड़तीस। दोनों में से कोई ग़लत नहीं। और असल में फँसी energy लगभग चालीस प्रतिशत efficiency बैठती है। बाक़ी गर्मी बनकर उड़ जाती है।

अब वह हिस्सा जो पूरे अंक वाले जवाब को आधे अंक वाले से अलग करता है। यह आँकड़ा चार साफ़ idealisations पर टिका है, और उन्हें नाम से गिनाना ख़ुद एक exam point है। पहला, माना जाता है कि pathway एक ही सुव्यवस्थित क्रम में चलती है। Glycolysis, फिर link reaction और Krebs cycle, फिर E T S, और हर step अगले को ठीक से खिलाता है।

दूसरा, माना जाता है कि glycolysis के दौरान cytoplasm में बनी N A D H ज्यों की त्यों mitochondrion में पहुँचाई जाती है और oxidative phosphorylation से गुज़रती है। तीसरा, माना जाता है कि किसी भी stage पर कोई intermediate किसी दूसरे molecule को बनाने के लिए नहीं खींचा जाता। और चौथा, माना जाता है कि glucose ही इकलौता substrate है, और बीच के बिंदुओं पर और कुछ नहीं घुसता।

और अब देखिए इस subtopic ने अभी-अभी आपको क्या सिखाया है। असली cells तीसरी और चौथी मान्यता लगातार तोड़ती हैं। यही तो वह amphibolic व्यवहार है जो हमने अभी बताया। Intermediates हर वक़्त खींचे जाते हैं, और दूसरे fuels हर वक़्त घुसते हैं। तो असली yield हमेशा अड़तीस से कुछ कम रहती है। अड़तीस को छत मानिए, गारंटी नहीं। यही एक वाक्य number रटने और उसे समझने के बीच का फ़र्क़ है।
इस subtopic में ठीक एक formula है, और फिर कुछ substituted cases। इन्हें ठीक से लिख लेते हैं।
यह रही definition।
और साथ में dimensional note भी रखिए। यह शुद्ध अनुपात है, dimensionless, कोई unit नहीं। आयतन बटा आयतन।
अब साफ़ मामला। Glucose, एक carbohydrate।
Coefficients पढ़िए। छह carbon dioxide निकली, छह oxygen ख़र्च हुई। छह बटा छह बराबर एक। इसीलिए carbohydrate पूरी table का reference point है।
अब एक fat। Tripalmitin, जो textbook का standard उदाहरण है।
इन numbers को एक पल देखिए। एक सौ पैंतालीस oxygen ख़र्च, लेकिन सिर्फ़ एक सौ दो carbon dioxide बाहर। Carbon dioxide के मुक़ाबले oxygen की माँग बहुत बड़ी है।
तो अनुपात निकलता है एक सौ दो बटा एक सौ पैंतालीस, यानी zero point seven zero three, यानी लगभग zero point seven। यह इत्तेफ़ाक़ नहीं है, और इसे अलग से रटना भी नहीं है। यह equation से ख़ुद निकल आता है।

और reference के लिए पूरा सेट। Carbohydrate बराबर एक। Protein zero point eight से zero point nine। Fat zero point seven। Organic acids एक से ऊपर, malic one point three three पर और oxalic चार पर। Anaerobic, infinity। लेकिन इन्हें ढीला पकड़िए, क्योंकि हम इन सबको एक ही idea से निकालने वाले हैं।

Example एक सीधा board question है, और यही बाक़ी सबका reference case है। एक अंकुरित होता गेहूँ का दाना जमा starch से respiration कर रहा है। Glucose के oxidation का overall equation लिखिए और उसका respiratory quotient निकालिए।
Board पर वही सिद्धांत है जिस पर हम दोनों examples में टिकेंगे। बाईं ओर oxygen-ग़रीब, दाईं ओर oxygen-अमीर।

Substrate पहचानकर शुरू कीजिए, क्योंकि यही हमेशा पहला क़दम है। Starch से glucose मिलता है, जो carbohydrate है। Balanced equation है glucose plus छह oxygen देता है छह carbon dioxide plus छह पानी। अब coefficients पढ़िए। निकली carbon dioxide छह। खपत हुई oxygen छह। तो R Q है छह बटा छह, यानी एक।
और निष्कर्ष शब्दों में लिखिए, क्योंकि marks उसी से मिलते हैं। R Q बराबर एक carbohydrate substrate की पहचान है।
Example दो एक C U E T और N E E T का speed trap है, और इसे लगभग दस सेकंड में हल करने के लिए बनाया गया है। तेल से भरा castor seed एक बंद respirometer में अंकुरित हो रहा है।
उसका R Q एक के मुक़ाबले क्या होगा, कारण सहित बताइए, और बिना कोई गणना किए। निर्देश पर ध्यान दीजिए। आपसे कुछ गिनने को कहा ही नहीं गया। आपसे fuel से तर्क करने को कहा गया है।

तो तर्क कीजिए। तेल यानी fat। Fat एक oxygen-ग़रीब, बहुत reduced molecule है। उसे पूरा oxidise करने के लिए बाहर से अतिरिक्त oxygen चाहिए। तो खपत हुई oxygen निकली carbon dioxide से ज़्यादा है। इसलिए R Q एक से कम है, आम fats के लिए लगभग zero point seven। तीन वाक्य, कोई गणित नहीं।

<curious> और यह रहा वह trap जिस पर यह सवाल असल में बना है। Students मान लेते हैं कि seed है, तो R Q बराबर एक। लेकिन यह सिर्फ़ starch वाले बीजों पर लागू होता है, जैसे गेहूँ और चावल। तेल वाले बीज, castor, सरसों, मूँगफली, R Q एक से कम देते हैं। R Q substrate तय करता है, अंग नहीं। जब भी सवाल किसी molecule के बजाय किसी संरचना का नाम ले, पूछिए कि उसके अंदर जल क्या रहा है।

board_events.text: The oxidation proceeds as: 2 C51H98O6 + 145 O2 gives 102 CO2 + 98 H2O. Read the coefficients directly: CO2 evolved = 102; O2 consumed = 145.
RQ = 102/145 = 0.703 $\approx$ 0.7. This confirms the rule of thumb that fats give an RQ of about 0.7 - well below 1, because so much oxygen must be supplied to burn the long, reduced carbon chains.
Example 4 [NEET High-Difficulty / Assertion-Reason]: the succulent
A: A succulent plant respiring stored organic acids can show an RQ greater than 1. R: Organic acids are oxygen-rich substrates, so their complete oxidation consumes less O2 than the CO2 it releases.

Many succulents (CAM plants) store malic acid overnight and respire it. Malic acid (RQ $\approx$ 1.33) and oxalic acid (RQ $\approx$ 4) are already partially oxidised - oxygen-rich - so very little external O2 is needed while CO2 continues to be released.
The CO2/O2 ratio therefore exceeds 1. A is true; R is true and correctly explains A. ANSWER: (a).
Contrast for depth: this is the MIRROR IMAGE of fat (RQ $\lt$ 1) - same logic, opposite direction, driven entirely by the oxygen content of the fuel.
Pitfall 1: 'all seeds give RQ = 1'
False. Starchy seeds give about 1; oily seeds (castor, mustard) give $\lt$ 1; some succulents and organic-acid tissues give $\gt$ 1. Always identify the SUBSTRATE first.
Pitfall 2: forgetting the anaerobic case
Anaerobic respiration has RQ = infinity (CO2 released, but no O2 consumed) - NOT 0. Zero would mean no CO2 at all.
Pitfall 3: mislabelling the pathway. 'Amphibolic' means catabolic AND anabolic - not 'occurs in both plants and animals'. Examiners love this trap.
Pitfall 4: treating 38 ATP as exact. It is an idealised ceiling; intermediate withdrawal (the amphibolic reality) and shuttle costs mean real yields are lower - about 36 or less.
PRO-TIP: for any RQ question, don't memorise values - reason from oxygen content in one glance.

O-poor fuel (fat) gives RQ $\lt$ 1. Balanced fuel (carbohydrate) gives RQ = 1. O-rich fuel (organic acid) gives RQ $\gt$ 1. No O2 used (anaerobic) gives RQ = infinity. One principle replaces the whole table. Memory aids: 'Fat is Lean on oxygen, so RQ is Low'; 'Acids are rich, so RQ is High'; 'No O2, infinite RQ'; 'Amphi = both ways'.
RESPIRATION IN PLANTS - everything on one board

GASEOUS EXCHANGE: plants have no respiratory organs. Routes: stomata (leaves), lenticels (woody stems), root surface from soil air. Why none are needed: each part looks after itself, short diffusion distances, continuous intercellular spaces, and a low demand. Aerenchyma supplies O2 to waterlogged roots.

GLYCOLYSIS (EMP pathway) - cytoplasm, in ALL living cells, O2-independent: glucose (6C) to 2 pyruvate (3C). Net 2 ATP + 2 NADH. Rate-limiting enzyme: PFK. ATP is invested twice, then harvested by substrate-level phosphorylation at two steps, in two trioses.

FERMENTATION - the point is to regenerate NAD+. Alcoholic (yeast): pyruvate to acetaldehyde + CO2, then to ethanol. Lactic (muscle): pyruvate to lactic acid, NO CO2. Net stays 2 ATP; less than 7% of glucose's energy is released.
LINK REACTION - mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex: pyruvate (3C) + CoA + NAD+ gives acetyl CoA (2C) + CO2 + NADH.

KREBS / TCA / CITRIC ACID CYCLE - matrix (cytosol in prokaryotes): acetyl CoA + OAA gives citrate. Per turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP, 2 CO2; per glucose, double it. Only substrate-level ATP step: succinyl-CoA to succinic acid. Only membrane-bound Krebs enzyme: succinate dehydrogenase (= ETS Complex II).

ETS - inner mitochondrial membrane: I NADH dehydrogenase, II succinate dehydrogenase, III cyt bc1, IV cyt c oxidase (to O2), V ATP synthase. Mobile carriers: ubiquinone, cytochrome c. Chemiosmosis: the proton gradient drives ATP synthase. NADH gives 3 ATP, FADH2 gives 2 ATP. O2 = terminal acceptor, forming H2O.

AMPHIBOLIC: respiration serves catabolism AND anabolism - acetyl CoA, alpha-ketoglutarate and OAA are withdrawn to build fats and amino acids. Substrates: fats (to glycerol + fatty acids) and proteins (to amino acids) all converge on ACETYL CoA.

RQ = CO2 evolved / O2 consumed, dimensionless. Carbohydrate = 1; protein 0.8 - 0.9; fat 0.7; organic acids $\gt$ 1 (malic 1.33, oxalic 4); anaerobic = infinity. BALANCE SHEET: 4 direct ATP + 10 NADH + 2 FADH2, giving net $\approx$ 38 ATP per glucose (about 36 with the shuttle); efficiency $\approx$ 40%.
Memory aids: 'Can I Keep Selling Sea Food Money?' (Krebs order) - '3 minus 2 = the FADH2 gap' - 'OAA goes round and comes round' - 'No O2, infinite RQ' - 'Amphi = both ways'.

segments.text: Example three is a N E E T calculation, and the whole difficulty is in not being intimidated by the formula. The oxidation of the fat tripalmitin is given. Calculate its respiratory quotient.
The board has both examples side by side, and putting them next to each other is the point. They are the same reasoning, running in opposite directions.

The reaction is two tripalmitin plus one hundred forty-five oxygen gives one hundred two carbon dioxide plus ninety-eight water. Now, you are not expected to balance this or to know the molecular formula. You are expected to read the coefficients directly. Carbon dioxide evolved is one hundred two. Oxygen consumed is one hundred forty-five. That is all you need from that intimidating equation.

So R Q is one hundred two over one hundred forty-five, which is zero point seven zero three, or approximately zero point seven. And this confirms the rule of thumb, that fats give an R Q of about zero point seven, well below one. And you already know why. So much oxygen must be supplied to burn the long, reduced carbon chains. The calculation and the principle agree, which is exactly what you want to see.
Example four is a high-difficulty assertion-reason, and it takes the same principle and runs it backwards.

The assertion. A succulent plant respiring stored organic acids can show an R Q greater than one. The reason. Organic acids are oxygen-rich substrates, so their complete oxidation consumes less oxygen than the carbon dioxide it releases.

Check the biology first. Many succulents, which are C A M plants, store malic acid overnight and respire it. That part is true, and it connects to what you know about C A M photosynthesis. Now the chemistry. Malic acid, with an R Q of about one point three three, and oxalic acid, with an R Q of about four, are already partially oxidised. They are oxygen-rich. So very little external oxygen is needed, while carbon dioxide continues to be released.

Therefore the carbon dioxide over oxygen ratio exceeds one. So the assertion is true. The reason is true. And the reason correctly explains the assertion, because the high internal oxygen of the substrate lowers the oxygen requirement and pushes R Q above one. The answer is option a.

<curious> And carry this contrast, because it is the deepest point in the subtopic. This is the mirror image of fat. Fat sits below one, organic acid sits above one, and it is the same logic running in opposite directions, driven entirely by the oxygen content of the fuel. If you hold that one contrast, you never need the table again.
Four pitfalls, and then the single principle that makes the R Q table unnecessary.

Pitfall one. All seeds give R Q equal to one. False, and we have already seen why. Starchy seeds give about one. Oily seeds, castor and mustard, give less than one. Some succulents and organic-acid tissues give more than one. Always identify the substrate first. The word seed tells you nothing about the fuel.
Pitfall two. Forgetting the anaerobic case.

Anaerobic respiration has R Q equal to infinity. Carbon dioxide is released, but no oxygen is consumed. It is not zero. And think about why the zero option is wrong, because that is what the examiner is testing. Zero would mean no carbon dioxide at all, which never happens in active respiration. Infinity comes from the denominator being zero, not the numerator.

Pitfall three. Mislabelling the pathway. Amphibolic means catabolic and anabolic. It does not mean occurs in both plants and animals. Examiners love this trap, because that option is a true statement about respiration. It is just not what the word means. Read the definition, not the vibe of the word.

Pitfall four. Treating thirty-eight A T P as exact. It is an idealised ceiling. Intermediate withdrawal, which is the amphibolic reality, and shuttle costs mean real yields are lower, about thirty-six or less. If a question asks you to comment on the figure, that is the comment.
<whisper> And now the pro-tip, which is the single most useful line in this subtopic. For any R Q question, do not memorise values. Reason from oxygen content in one glance.

Here it is in full. Oxygen-poor fuel, that is fat, gives R Q less than one. Balanced fuel, that is carbohydrate, gives R Q equal to one. Oxygen-rich fuel, that is organic acid, gives R Q greater than one. And no oxygen used at all, that is anaerobic, gives R Q equal to infinity. One principle replaces the entire table. If you want the words to hang it on, try these. Fat is lean on oxygen, so R Q is low. Acids are rich, so R Q is high. No oxygen, infinite R Q. And amphi means both ways, breakdown and build-up on one pathway.
That closes the chapter. Here is everything on one board, in the order you will need it in the exam hall.

Gaseous exchange. Plants have no respiratory organs. The routes are stomata in leaves, lenticels in woody stems, and the root surface drawing on soil air. And know why no organs are needed. Each part looks after itself, diffusion distances are short, intercellular spaces are continuous, and demand is low. Aerenchyma is the exception that proves the rule, supplying oxygen to waterlogged roots.

Glycolysis, the E M P pathway. Cytoplasm, in all living cells, and independent of oxygen. Glucose with six carbons becomes two pyruvate with three each. Net two A T P and two N A D H. The rate-limiting enzyme is P F K. A T P is invested twice, then harvested by substrate-level phosphorylation at two steps, in two trioses.

Fermentation. Remember the point of it. It exists to regenerate N A D plus, not to make A T P. Alcoholic, in yeast, goes pyruvate to acetaldehyde plus carbon dioxide, then to ethanol. Lactic, in muscle, goes pyruvate straight to lactic acid, with no carbon dioxide at all. Net stays at two A T P, and less than seven percent of glucose's energy is released.
The link reaction. Mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Pyruvate plus coenzyme A plus N A D plus gives acetyl coenzyme A plus carbon dioxide plus N A D H.

Krebs, also called T C A, also called the citric acid cycle. Matrix, or cytosol in prokaryotes. Acetyl coenzyme A plus O A A gives citrate. Per turn, three N A D H, one F A D H two, one A T P and two carbon dioxide. Per glucose, double it. The only substrate-level A T P step is succinyl coenzyme A to succinic acid. And the only membrane-bound Krebs enzyme is succinate dehydrogenase, which is E T S complex two.

The E T S, on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Complex one, N A D H dehydrogenase. Two, succinate dehydrogenase. Three, cytochrome b c one. Four, cytochrome c oxidase, which hands electrons to oxygen. Five, A T P synthase. Mobile carriers, ubiquinone and cytochrome c. Chemiosmosis means the proton gradient drives A T P synthase. N A D H gives three A T P, F A D H two gives two. Oxygen is the terminal acceptor, forming water.

Amphibolic. Respiration serves catabolism and anabolism at once. Acetyl coenzyme A, alpha-ketoglutarate and O A A are withdrawn to build fats and amino acids. And the substrates. Fats break to glycerol plus fatty acids, proteins to amino acids, and all of them converge on acetyl coenzyme A.

And R Q. Carbon dioxide evolved over oxygen consumed, dimensionless. Carbohydrate one, protein zero point eight to zero point nine, fat zero point seven, organic acids above one with malic at one point three three and oxalic at four, and anaerobic infinity. The balance sheet. Four direct A T P, ten N A D H, two F A D H two, giving a net of about thirty-eight A T P per glucose, or about thirty-six with the shuttle, at roughly forty percent efficiency.

And the memory aids, all in one place. Can I Keep Selling Sea Food Money, for the Krebs order. Three minus two is the F A D H two gap. O A A goes round and comes round. No oxygen, infinite R Q. And amphi means both ways. That is the whole chapter. Every number in it came from a mechanism, so if a figure slips your mind in the hall, go back to the mechanism and rebuild it.
Example तीन एक N E E T calculation है, और पूरी कठिनाई सिर्फ़ formula से न घबराने में है। Tripalmitin नाम के fat का oxidation दिया गया है। उसका respiratory quotient निकालिए।
Board पर दोनों examples साथ-साथ हैं, और उन्हें अगल-बगल रखना ही असल बात है। दोनों में तर्क वही है, बस दिशाएँ उल्टी हैं।

Reaction है दो tripalmitin plus एक सौ पैंतालीस oxygen देता है एक सौ दो carbon dioxide plus अट्ठानबे पानी। अब, आपसे इसे balance करने या molecular formula याद रखने की उम्मीद नहीं है। आपसे उम्मीद है कि आप coefficients सीधे पढ़ लें। निकली carbon dioxide एक सौ दो। खपत हुई oxygen एक सौ पैंतालीस। उस डरावने equation से आपको बस इतना ही चाहिए।

तो R Q है एक सौ दो बटा एक सौ पैंतालीस, यानी zero point seven zero three, यानी लगभग zero point seven। और यह उस rule of thumb की पुष्टि करता है कि fats लगभग zero point seven R Q देते हैं, एक से काफ़ी नीचे। और वजह आप जानते ही हैं। लंबी, reduced carbon chains जलाने के लिए इतनी सारी oxygen देनी पड़ती है। गणना और सिद्धांत सहमत हैं, और यही देखना आप चाहते हैं।
Example चार एक high-difficulty assertion-reason है, और यह उसी सिद्धांत को उल्टी दिशा में चलाता है।

Assertion। जमा किए हुए organic acids से respiration करता succulent पौधा एक से ज़्यादा R Q दिखा सकता है। Reason। Organic acids oxygen से भरपूर substrates हैं, इसलिए उनके पूरे oxidation में जितनी carbon dioxide निकलती है, उससे कम oxygen खर्च होती है।
